chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Abzārī al-Kunāsī, from al-Ḥārith ibn al-Mughīrah, who said:

I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: What do you think—if a man were to come to the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم and say, “By Allah, I do not know whether you are a Prophet or not,” would he accept that from him?
He عليه السلام said: “No. Rather, he would kill him. If he had accepted that, no hypocrite would ever have entered Islam.”

key_terms.أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام, the one being asked
key_terms.أَنَبِيٌّ: a Prophet; the core subject of the speaker’s doubt
key_terms.النَّبِيَّ: the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم whose prophethood is being questioned
key_terms.مُنَافِقٌ: a hypocrite; one who outwardly enters Islam while inwardly concealing disbelief
key_terms.يَقْبَلُ: accept; whether such a statement would be accepted from the speaker
key_terms.يَقْتُلُهُ: he would kill him; the legal consequence mentioned in the report

ai.seo_question: What does Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām say about someone who openly doubts the Prophet’s prophethood?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the ruling concerning one who openly expresses doubt about the prophethood of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم after the truth has been established. Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام states that such a statement would not be accepted, and explains that accepting it would open the door for hypocrisy to enter Islam without restraint.
